mappings.note: States the sign of each coordinate in each of the four quadrants -- the second clause of LO-1, given in full.
Both coordinates negative identifies the third quadrant. The same sign rule as qid:706520, reduced to one case.
Matches all four quadrants to their sign pairs in one item -- LO-1's sign rule tested exhaustively.
The 3-4-5 distance from the origin. A single application of the distance formula, LO-4.
Why the formula cannot return a negative value: squares then the positive root. That is understanding the formula itself, LO-4, not a computation.
Distance between (1,2) and (4,6) with working shown. LO-4, the plain computational form.
Derives the distance formula from the right triangle whose legs are the coordinate differences -- where the formula comes from, LO-4.
Symmetry of the distance formula, justified by the squaring of the differences. Still LO-4: both statements are about the formula's structure.
Three side lengths from the distance formula, then classifying the triangle by comparing them. LO-4; no area formula is involved, so C-5.1 does not apply.
Distance of (8,6) from the origin, the special case where one point is (0,0). LO-4.
Collinearity decided by AB+BC=AC, so three distance computations. LO-4 used as a test rather than as an answer in itself.
Proves two sides equal and the Pythagoras relation holds, both from the distance formula. LO-4, at proof length.
One direct application of the midpoint formula. LO-5.
Inverts the midpoint formula to recover the missing endpoint. Still LO-5, but run backwards, which is what distinguishes it from qid:706532.
False, and the counterexample needs endpoints in different quadrants: the midpoint outcome (LO-5) tested against the quadrant sign rule (LO-1).
Why the average gives the halfway point, and whether the idea generalises to an arbitrary ratio. The reasoning behind LO-5, and its extension.
Midpoint of (-3,7) and (5,-1), with mixed signs to handle. LO-5.
The ordinate of any point on the x-axis is zero -- LO-2's 'including points that lie on an axis'. LO-1 would apply if a quadrant were being named.
The abscissa of any point on the y-axis is zero. The mirror of qid:706537, same LO-2 on-axis clause.
Explains that the quadrants are the four regions and the axes are their boundaries (LO-1), so an on-axis point belongs to none (LO-2's on-axis case).

The assertion wrongly places (0,7) in the first quadrant; the refutation is that a zero abscissa puts it on the y-axis (LO-2), which is in no quadrant (LO-1). The reason given is true but does not support the assertion.
Gap-fill for the abscissa of a point on the y-axis. Same LO-2 on-axis fact as qid:706538.
Image of (4,-3) in the x-axis. LO-3's first case, with the sign of the ordinate reversed.
All three reflections stated as coordinate rules. LO-3 names the two axis reflections; the origin case is their composition and is covered in the same answer.
Assertion and reason both concern reflection in the y-axis reversing the abscissa -- LO-3's second case.
Gives the three images of P(a,b) (LO-3) and locates each in its quadrant, explaining how the four points sit symmetrically about the axes (LO-1's sign rule).
Matches the three reflections plus the identity to their images. LO-3 tested across all its cases at once.
